theme: Moses recounts the journey, covenant history
readingInstruction: Read Deuteronomy 1:1-3:29. A new book begins, and it is a series of sermons by Moses. Notice how he looks backward to the journey from Sinai, and what he says to the new generation about what their parents did.
settingTheScene: Deuteronomy means “second law.” It takes place on the plains of Moab, in the last weeks of Moses’ life. Forty years have passed since the exodus. A new generation, most of whom were children or unborn at Sinai, stands ready to cross the Jordan. Moses preaches to them in a series of speeches. The first section, which you read today, is a historical review: it recalls how God led Israel from Horeb to this place, and why they are here and not in the land already.
observation: “It is eleven days” journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea’ (1:2).
“The LORD our God said to us in Horeb, You have stayed long enough at this mountain” (1:6).
Moses recounts how he appointed leaders to share the burden of judging (1:9-18).
The people refused to enter the land: “Because the LORD hated us he has brought us out of the land of Egypt” (1:27).
“The LORD your God… carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went” (1:31).
Because of their unbelief, the LORD swore that none of that generation would see the land, except Caleb (1:34-36).
Moses was also barred from entering because of the people (1:37; 3:23-27).
God gives victories over Sihon and Og, and Moses sees the land from Mount Pisgah (2:26-3:29).
interpretation:
Moses begins by looking back, and what he says is a lesson in the right use of memory. He remembers the failures honestly, including his own burden and the people’s refusal. But he also remembers God’s care. The most beautiful line is 1:31: “in the wilderness, where you saw how the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son.” Behind the story of rebellion and judgment, there was a father carrying his child.

The review has a purpose. The new generation needs to understand why they are standing east of the Jordan, and why the land is a gift and not an achievement. If they think the land is theirs by right, they will repeat their fathers’ mistake. Moses tells the story so that they will learn to trust.

It also reveals the heart of the old generation’s sin. They said, “Because the LORD hated us he has brought us out of Egypt.” This is a shocking accusation. The very act of rescue became evidence of hatred in their minds. It is a picture of what unbelief does. It takes God’s love and turns it inside out.

Moses’ mention of his own exclusion from the land shows an honesty in leadership. He does not hide his failure or pretend that it was unjust. He says that God was angry with him “on your account,” and that he pleaded for mercy and was refused. The leader shares the consequences of the people’s sin, and in that sense he points beyond himself to one who would bear them fully.

The chapters end with Moses on the mountain, looking over the land he will not enter, and with the command to charge and encourage Joshua. The torch is passed. The people will go in, and Moses will not. But God will be with Joshua.
connection: Stephen’s speech in Acts 7 retells this history, and Paul preaches a similar summary in Acts 13:18, citing Deuteronomy 1:31: “he put up with them in the wilderness.” Isaiah 63:9 says, “In all their affliction he was afflicted… he lifted them up and carried them all the days of old.” Jesus said, “Come to me… and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Moses looks at the land from afar, as Hebrews 11:13 says of all the faithful.
application:
Take time to remember how God has carried you. Write down two or three instances.

Ask whether you have ever interpreted God’s care as hostility, and tell him about it.

Think about those you are leading or teaching. How might you pass on what God has done?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for carrying you as a father carries his son, naming a time you did not know it.
Confess where you mistook his love for hatred.
Ask him to teach you to remember his works and pass them on.
